'''Henri Boris Kagan''' ({{IPA|fr|ɑ̃ʁi kaɡɑ̃|lang}}; born 15 December 1930) is a French chemist. He is currently an [[emeritus professor]] at the [[Paris-Saclay University|Université Paris-Saclay]] in [[France]]. He is widely recognized as a pioneer in the field of [[asymmetric catalysis]]. His discoveries have had far-reaching impacts on the [[pharmaceutical industry]].<ref>{{Cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XPUZAAAAIAAJ&q=%22Kagan,+henri%22+1930 |title = Who's who in Western Europe|isbn = 978-0-900332-61-6|year = 1981| publisher=International Biographical Centre }}</ref> 

In 2026, he was jointly awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] with [[Kensō Soai]] "for the discovery of non-linear effects and [[autocatalysis]] in asymmetric organic synthesis."<ref name=Nobel>{{Cite web |title=Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026 |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2026/press-release/ |access-date=7 October 2026 |website=NobelPrize.org |language=en-US |publisher=[[Nobel Foundation]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20261007095246/https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2026/press-release/ |archive-date=7 October 2026 |url-status=live}}</ref>

== Early life and education ==
Kagan was born on 15 December 1930 in [[Boulogne-Billancourt]], France,<ref name="JVL">{{cite web |title=Henri Kagan |url= https://jewishvirtuallibrary.org/henri-kagan |website=[[Jewish Virtual Library]] |access-date=7 October 2026}}</ref> to a [[Ashkenazi Jewish|Jewish]] family who survived [[World War II]] by hiding in a village in the south of France under assumed names.<ref name="JVL"/><ref>{{cite news |title=French Jewish chemist Henri Kagan, Japan's Kenso Soai win Nobel Prize for solving 'mirror image' mystery |url=https://www.timesofisrael.com/nobel-prize-in-chemistry-awarded-for-research-solving-mirror-image-mystery/ |access-date=7 October 2026 |work=[[The Times of Israel]] |date=7 October 2026}}</ref> He graduated from the [[University of Paris|Sorbonne]] and [[École nationale supérieure de chimie de Paris]] (in 1954). He subsequently completed his PhD under Jean Jacques at the [[Collège de France]] in 1960, researching steroid chemistry and [[stereochemistry]]. Subsequently, he was a research associate with Alain Horeau. In 1968, Kagan established a laboratory at [[Orsay]]. He became an [[emeritus professor]] at the [[Université Paris-Saclay]] in 1999.<ref name="JVL"/><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.europe1.fr/sciences/portrait-qui-est-henri-kagan-le-francais-de-95-ans-laureat-du-prix-nobel-de-chimie-1129769|title=Qui est Henri Kagan, le Français de 95 ans lauréat du prix Nobel de chimie ?|website=europe1.fr}}</ref>

== Academic career ==
Kagan moved to [[Université Paris-Sud]], [[Orsay]] where he became a professor.  A landmark in his research was the development of C<sub>2</sub>-symmetric ligands, e.g., [[DIOP]] for [[asymmetric catalysis]].<ref>{{cite journal
| author = Henri B. Kagan, Dang-Tuan-Phat
| title =  Asymmetric catalytic reduction with transition metal complexes. I. Catalytic system of rhodium(I) with (−)-2,3-0-isopropylidene-2,3-dihydroxy-1,4-bis(diphenylphosphino)butane, a new chiral diphosphine
| journal = Journal of the American Chemical Society
| volume = 94
| issue = 18
| year = 1972
| doi =  10.1021/ja00773a028
| pages =  6429–6433| bibcode = 1972JAChS..94.6429K
}}</ref><ref name=":2">{{cite news|url=https://new.societechimiquedefrance.fr/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/2013-377-sept.-p7-Balavoine_HD.pdf|author=Gilbert Balavoine|title=Sur la route d'Henri Kagan, dialogue…|publisher=l’actualité chimique|date=September 2013|access-date=|pages=7–10}}</ref> This discovery led to the discovery of many related ligands that support [[catalyst]]s used in a variety of practical applications.<ref>{{cite news |title=Who are Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai, the scientists awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry?. |url=https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/education/news/who-are-henri-kagan-and-kens-soai-the-scientists-awarded-the-2026-nobel-prize-in-chemistry/articleshow/134763141.cms |access-date=7 October 2026 |work=[[Times of India]] |date=7 October 2026}}</ref>

In 1986, Kagan observed the first examples of [[Non-linear effects in enantioselective synthesis|nonlinear effects]]<ref name=":2" /> in asymmetric catalysis and developed  mathematical models to describe the behavior of such catalysts.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Puchot |first1=C. |last2=Samuel |first2=O. |last3=Dunach |first3=E. |last4=Zhao |first4=S. |last5=Agami |first5=C. |last6=Kagan |first6=H. B. |date=1986 |title=Nonlinear effects in asymmetric synthesis. Examples in asymmetric oxidations and aldolization reactions |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00269a036 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=108 |issue=9 |pages=2353–2357 |doi=10.1021/ja00269a036 |issn=0002-7863 |pmid=22175583 |bibcode=1986JAChS.108.2353P |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220721075328/https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00269a036 |archive-date=21 July 2022 |access-date=15 October 2024 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":2" /> This result was a major discovery, making non-linear effects a field of chemistry in its own right: not only are they a tool for understanding [[molecular mechanics|molecular mechanisms]], but they are also discussed in the context of the [[abiogenesis|origin of life]] (asymmetric amplification).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Guillaneux |first1=Denis |last2=Zhao |first2=Shu-Hai |last3=Samuel |first3=Odile |last4=Rainford |first4=David |last5=Kagan |first5=Henri B. |date=October 1994 |title=Nonlinear Effects in Asymmetric Catalysis |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00100a004 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |language=en |volume=116 |issue=21 |pages=9430–9439 |doi=10.1021/ja00100a004 |bibcode=1994JAChS.116.9430G |issn=0002-7863 |url-access=subscription |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220809141934/https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00100a004 |archive-date=9 August 2022 |access-date=15 April 2025 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":2" /> For this work he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2026.<ref name=Nobel/>

==Honors and awards==
Kagan is a member of the [[French Academy of Sciences]], foreign member of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] in 1994, Fellow of [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] in 2003 and honorary member of the [[Chemical Research Society of India]].<ref name=":12" />

He has won many awards in the field including:

* 1967: [[Joseph Achille Le Bel|Le Bel]] Prize of the [[Société chimique de France]]<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |url=https://www.chemie.de/lexikon/Henri_Kagan.html|title=Henri Kagan|website=chemie.de|archive-date=}}</ref>
* 1968: [[Auguste André Thomas Cahours|Cahours]] Prize of the [[French Academy of Sciences]]<ref name=":12" />
* 1974: [[Centre national de la recherche scientifique|Silver Medal of the French National Scientific Research Center]]<ref name=":12" />
* 1976: Raymond Berr Prize<ref name=":12" />
* 1989: ''Prix du rayonnement français<ref name=":12" />''
* 1990: [[Prelog Medal]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 1991: [[August-Wihelm-von Hoffman Medal|August-Wilhelm-von Hofmann Medal]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 1998: [[Nagoya]] Gold Medal in Organic Chemistry''<ref name=":12" />''<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://ocyrd.csj.jp/nagoya_medalseminer/medal_award_gold/|title=Nagoya Gold Medal Recipients|website=ocyrd.csj.jp}}</ref>
* 1998: Yamada Prize of the Japan Research Foundation for Optically Active Compounds''<ref name=":12" />''
* 1999: [[Tetrahedron Prize|Tetrahedron Prize for Creativity in Organic Chemistry]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 1999: Centenary Prize of the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 2001: [[Wolf Prize in Chemistry]] (with [[Ryōji Noyori]] and [[Karl Barry Sharpless]])''<ref name=":12" />''<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://wolffund.org.il/henri-b-kagan/|title=Henri B. Kagan|website=wolffund.org.il |date=10 December 2018 }}</ref>
* 2002: Grand Prize of the [[Maison de la Chimie]] Foundation''<ref name=":12" />''<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://fondation.maisondelachimie.com/les-actions/les-prix-de-la-fondation/grand-prix-de-la-fondation/les-anciens-laureats/|title=Les anciens lauréats|website=fondation.maisondelachimie.com}}</ref>
* 2002: [[JSPS Award for Eminent Scientists]] of the [[Japan Society for the Promotion of Science]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 2002: [[Ryoji Noyori Prize]]''<ref name=":12" />''
* 2005: [[The Franklin Institute Awards|Benjamin Franklin Medal]] (Bower Award and Prize for Achievement in Science)<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://fi.edu/en/awards/laureates/henri-b-kagan|title=Henri B. Kagan|website=fi.edu |date=13 January 2014 }}</ref>
* 2013: Lavoisier Medal of the [[Société chimique de France]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Henri B. Kagan – The Franklin Institute Awards – Laureate Database|url=http://www.fi.edu/winners/2005/kagan_henri.faw?winner_id=4388|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120205182004/http://www.fi.edu/winners/2005/kagan_henri.faw?winner_id=4388|archive-date=5 February 2012|access-date=7 October 2026|website=www.fi.edu|url-status=dead}}</ref>
* 2026: [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] (with [[Kensō Soai]])<ref name="Nobel" />

===Nobel Prize in Chemistry===
In 2001, there was some controversy when Kagan was not awarded the [[Nobel Prize]] that year, which had been shared by [[K. Barry Sharpless]] of the [[Scripps Research Institute]] in La Jolla, California, [[Ryōji Noyori]] of [[Nagoya University]], Japan, and [[William S. Knowles]], formerly of [[Monsanto Company]] in St Louis, Missouri, for work on catalytic asymmetric synthesis. Several French scientists voiced their protests. The French minister for science, [[Roger-Gérard Schwartzenberg]], thought that Kagan, as a pioneer of the field, should also have been honoured. However, the prize can be given to a maximum of three people.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Goodman |first=Sally |date=2001 |title=French Nobel protest makes chemist a cause célèbre |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=414 |issue=6861 |pages=239 |doi=10.1038/35104765 |pmid=11713488 |issn=1476-4687|bibcode=2001Natur.414..239G |doi-access=free }}</ref> 

On 7 October 2026, Kagan, along with [[Kensō Soai|Kenso Soai]], was awarded the [[Nobel Prize in Chemistry]] “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”.<ref name=Nobel/><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Larousserie |first1=David |url=https://www.lemonde.fr/en/science/article/2026/10/07/french-scientist-henri-kagan-wins-long-awaited-nobel-prize-in-chemistry_6758364_10.html|title=French scientist Henri Kagan wins long-awaited Nobel Prize in Chemistry|website=lemonde.fr}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6ly038jg0d4o|title=Chemistry Nobel awarded for solving mystery of life's asymmetry|website=bbc.com}}</ref>

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences linked the award to the emergence of [[homochirality]], the predominance of one mirror-image form of a molecule. Its announcement identified Kagan's 1986 discovery as a way of producing a larger excess of one mirror-image form than previously thought possible, and described the laureates' discoveries as important for designing reactions used in pharmaceutical manufacture.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2026 – Press release |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/2026/press-release/ |website=NobelPrize.org |date=7 October 2026 |access-date=10 October 2026}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Addicoat |first1=Matthew |editor-first1=Paul |editor-last1=Rincon |url=https://theconversation.com/nobel-prize-in-chemistry-awarded-for-work-on-mirror-image-molecules-293816|title=Nobel prize in chemistry awarded for work on mirror-image molecules|website=theconversation.com |doi=10.64628/AB.vydgfju9u |url-access=subscription }}</ref>
